knowledge.label: Statistics
knowledge.text: The foundations: describing data, quantifying uncertainty and testing whether a pattern is real.

children.label: Hypothesis testing
children.text:
Start from a null hypothesis (no effect), compute a test statistic, and ask how surprising it would be if the null were true. That probability is the p-value.

  • t-test: compare means
  • Chi-squared: compare category counts
  • Small p-value = evidence against the null, not proof of the alternative

children.label: Distributions
children.text:
The shape of a variable decides which summaries and tests are valid.

  • Normal: symmetric; mean and SD describe it
  • Skewed: use median and IQR, consider a log transform
  • Poisson: counts of events per interval

children.label: Correlation
children.text:
• Pearson: strength of a linear relationship
  • Spearman: rank-based, catches any monotonic relationship and resists outliers
  • Correlation is not causation, and near-zero correlation doesn't rule out a curved relationship

knowledge.label: EDA
knowledge.text: Exploring data before modelling it: what's there, what's broken, and what relates to the target.

children.label: Data profiling
children.text:
Look at every column on its own before asking what it predicts.

  • Shape, dtypes, memory
  • Missing values and duplicates
  • Cardinality of categoricals
  • Ranges and impossible values

children.label: Visualisation
children.text:
• One variable: histogram, box plot, bar chart
  • Two variables: scatter, grouped bars, heatmap
  • Over time: line plots, seasonal breakdowns, autocorrelation (ACF)

children.label: Outliers & label checks
children.text: Decide whether unusual values are errors, rare-but-real, or a sign the labels themselves are inconsistent. In the accidents data, two words for the same weather had very different severe rates, which traced back to a change in how the data was recorded.

knowledge.label: Preprocessing
knowledge.text: The bridge between analysis and modelling: turning raw columns and raw text into inputs a model can learn from.

children.label: Data cleaning
children.text:
• Fix types (dates, categories)
  • Handle missing values: drop, impute, or flag
  • Merge sources with matching columns
  • Remove leakage columns that wouldn't exist at prediction time

children.label: Feature engineering
children.text: Build better inputs from raw ones using domain knowledge: ratios, counts, time-since, hour and day-of-week from timestamps. Often worth more than changing the algorithm.

children.label: Scaling & encoding
children.text:
• Z-score: (x − μ) / σ, fit on train only
  • Needed for: gradient descent, regularised models, neural nets
  • Not needed for: decision trees, XGBoost
  • Encoding: one-hot for nominal categories

children.label: Text cleaning (regex)
children.text:
First NLP step: normalise the raw text.

  • Lowercase
  • Replace money, numbers, emails, URLs with tokens (moneytoken, numtoken)
  • Strip list markers like (a), (ii)
  • Remove punctuation, collapse spaces

children.label: Tokenise & lemmatise
children.text:
• Tokenisation: split text into words
  • Tagging: label each token noun, verb, etc.
  • Lemmatisation: reduce to base form (indemnified → indemnify)
  • Stop words: drop very common words that carry little meaning

Done with spaCy, in batches.

children.label: TF-IDF
children.text:
Turns text into numbers. Each word's weight = how often it appears in this document × how rare it is across all documents.

  • Sublinear TF: 1 + log(count), so 10 repeats count ~2×, not 10×
  • n-grams (1–3): keeps short phrases like "governing law"
  • min_df / max_df: drop words too rare or too common
  • L2 norm: long and short documents become comparable

knowledge.label: ML Models
knowledge.text: Supervised models from linear regression to boosted trees, plus unsupervised anomaly detection.

children.label: Linear regression
children.text:
Model: f = w·x + b

Cost: squared error, J = (1/2m) Σ (f − y)²

  • Convex, so gradient descent finds the single minimum
  • Update: w := w − α ∂J/∂w (all weights simultaneously)
  • Report RMSE (same units as y), MAE, R²

children.label: Logistic regression
children.text:
Model: f = sigmoid(w·x + b), an output between 0 and 1

Cost: log loss, which is convex (squared error with a sigmoid is not)

  • Decision boundary where w·x + b = 0
  • Moving the threshold trades precision against recall
  • sklearn applies L2 by default; C = 1/λ

children.label: Multiclass (softmax)
children.text:
Extends logistic regression to N classes. Softmax turns N scores into probabilities that sum to 1; the loss is −log(probability of the true class).

sklearn's LogisticRegression uses this automatically for more than two classes.

children.label: Bias & variance
children.text:
• High bias (underfit): train and validation error both high
  • High variance (overfit): train error low, validation much higher
  • More data fixes variance, not bias
  • Learning curves show which one you have

The trade-off: more model complexity lowers bias but raises variance.

children.label: Regularisation
children.text:
Adds a penalty on large weights to the cost, so the model can't contort itself to fit noise.

  • L2 (Ridge): λ Σ w², shrinks weights
  • L1 (Lasso): λ Σ |w|, drives some to exactly 0
  • Bigger λ = simpler model; don't penalise b
  • Pick λ at the bottom of the validation-error curve

children.label: Decision trees
children.text:
Split the data with yes/no questions, picking each split by the biggest drop in impurity (entropy / information gain, or Gini).

  • No scaling needed, handles non-linear patterns
  • Overfits easily: control with max_depth, min_samples_leaf
  • Easy to explain: feature importance, readable rules

children.label: XGBoost
children.text:
How it differs from one decision tree: it builds hundreds of small trees in sequence, each one trained to fix the errors the previous trees made (gradient boosting).

  • Single tree: one model, high variance, easy to read
  • Random forest: many trees in parallel, averaged (bagging) → lowers variance
  • XGBoost: trees in sequence (boosting) → lowers bias, with built-in regularisation to control variance

Usually the strongest model on tabular data.

children.label: Anomaly detection
children.text:
Unsupervised: no labels saying what's abnormal. Learn what normal looks like, then flag points far from it.

  • Remove expected patterns first (time of day, weekday, season)
  • Score what's left: z-scores, Isolation Forest, residuals from a forecast
  • Hard part is evaluation, since there's no ground truth

projects.label: US Accidents
projects.summary: Which weather, time-of-day and road features predict whether a US road accident will be severe? 7.7 million accidents, staged EDA, feature engineering, decision tree and XGBoost classifiers, error analysis, and a Power BI dashboard.

projects.label: Legal Clause NLP
projects.summary: Classify contract clauses into 100 types (LEDGAR / LexGLUE). Regex cleaning, spaCy lemmatisation, TF-IDF with n-grams, multiclass softmax logistic regression, and error analysis showing most mistakes are near-synonym labels.

projects.label: GB Grid Anomalies
projects.summary: In progress. Finding half-hours when GB national electricity demand (NESO, 2018–2023) is unusually high or low for its time of day, weekday and season, using unsupervised anomaly detection.
